content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present a federated learning framework that allows clients to generate synthetic data samples. Instead of the raw data, the clients only share the latent variable generated by local VAE. Meanwhile, the server is responsible for aggregating the model iterates and matching the clients. The authors also conduct extensive experiments in comparison with existing works.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The idea of sharing data representation instead of raw data is interesting. It is aligned with the design goal of federated learning in minimizing the data exposure. The algorithm also contains some novel components like client matching that can help balance the clients’ datasets. The experimental results indicate better performance than existing federated learning methods.

Weakness:
1. My main concern on this paper is the adoption of Gaussian mechanism on the latent means sharing. Simply applying Gaussian mechanism on this part doesn’t provide any form of privacy guarantees for the entire algorithm because other parts of the algorithm like preliminary training are still non-private and may lead to privacy leakage. 
2. The number of clients in the experiments is not large enough. In Table 1, the algorithms are tested with only 10 clients and the number of clients is still less than 50 in Table 2. These choices of the number of clients are not compatible with the setting in federated learning where data is distributed across larger number of clients.  Therefore, I recommend the authors to test and compare the algorithms with at least 100 clients.
3. The authors are not clear about the privacy parameters of the experiments. They mention that “there is abundant room for lower privacy budget $\epsilon$” at the end of page 7, does this mean the latent means computation is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP with $\epsilon ≤ 0.5$ for all experiments? If so, it would be better if the authors can state it clearly in the paper.

Question:

I am wondering if the authors can provide more details on the data partition in the experiments. Are the test and training datasets of the same client coming from the same distribution? For example, if the training dataset of client $i$ only contains datapoints from 4 out of 10 classes, does this mean the datapoints in the client $i$'s test dataset are also constrained in the same classes?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well written and organized. The authors also provide plenty of details for the experiments.

Novelty: The application of Gaussian mechanism does not constitute enough novelty since it does not provide any privacy guarantees over the entire algorithm. The other parts of the algorithm include some novel design ideas such as clients matching, but the general ideas are similar to existing FL data augmentation methods.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The authors give a FL algorithm that allows the client to generate synthetic datapoints with latent mean sharing. The idea is interesting, and the presentation is clear. However, I am concerned about the novelty of this paper may not be enough given DP mean sharing part is a straightforward application of Gaussian mechanism and there is still no privacy guarantee for the entire algorithm. 

I am willing to raise my score if the authors can address my concerns and questions.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work introduces a new FL framework called FedDPMS that utilizes an encoder and decoder to create synthetic data to improve utility in heterogeneous setting. Empirical evaluation on three image datasets show that the proposed method outperforms prior baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This work proposes a novel method to tackle data heterogeneity in FL.
- The empirical results look impressive.

Weaknesses:
- The proposed method communicates much more information than prior methods do (e.g. FedAvg, FedProx). FedDPMS also requires an additional decoder compared to prior methods. Therefore, it is not clear that whether the improvement of performance is coming from more information communicated between the clients and servers or the proposed method itself.
- Although the authors apply GM to the mean of latent variable, it is not convincing that the method is DP. Specifically, as the authors mentioned, the server holds a set that contains the indices of $n$ most abundant classes from any client $i$. The index set itself still reveals private information of the local clients. While it is not clear what the privacy formulation is considered in this work, the current algorithm still could not be considered as differentially private (only the mean of latent variable is privatized, not the models and index set communicated between server and client). Therefore, since the proposed model is using additional sensitive private information of the local data compared to prior works, the authors should account for the privacy for all variables communicated between the server and the clients and compare with the private version of prior works so that the results would be more convincing.
- Related to the previous point, formal privacy guarantee could strengthen the paper.
- The empirical results is only on image datasets right now. Could the authors show similarly results on an NLP dataset to demonstrate that the power of this method is not limited to specific structured data?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written and the proposed method is novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work proposes a novel method to handle data heterogeneity in FL. While the empirical results look good, the privacy argument is not well supported. Theoretical guarantees would also strengthen this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed a federated learning framework which synthesizing data by sharing locally trained auto-encoder and latent code. To protect local data privacy, the latent code is noised before shared to the public. These synthetic data is used for local training to boost local performance as well as global model performance.  Experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 show improvements over the other FL methods which do not augment data for local training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Utilizing auto-encoder to do data augmentation for federated learning is interesting.
2. The method is clearly written, and theoretical analysis is through.
3. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed method both qualitatively and quantitatively. The authors also do thorough ablation studies. 
4. Source codes are provided.

Weakness:
1. Although the methods add noise to protect privacy on the shared latent code, the iterative exchange of locally trained model parameters (encoder and classifier) have been shown to be highly susceptible to privacy leakage: [1] [2] demonstrated the ability to obtain local private data from publicly shared gradients. It will be meaningless to add protection on the shared latent code if there is privacy leakage caused by model parameters sharing. The authors should consider adding a differential privacy module for the shared parameters as well.
2. I am confused with the noisy latent means: in 3.4 it is not clear how each symbol (e.g. \epsilon, \sigma, \delta) in DP is associated with your case, analysis in A.7 and A.8 cannot clarify this either. I would expect more detailed explanation about the meaning of each symbol in your case and the details of the privacy cost calculation.


[1] Deep leakage from gradients.
[2] Inverting Gradients--How easy is it to break privacy in federated learning?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality: good.
Clarity: good.
Originality: generality good.
content.summary_of_the_review: My concern is mainly about the privacy analysis: how the noisy latent means satisfied  DP guarantee. I also doubt the main contribution of "differentially private synthetic data" considering the privacy leakage caused by iterative model parameters sharing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper sets out to study the non-iid setting in federated learning and to address its effects by enabling the clients to share data (specifically via the means of some learnt latent representation). The proposed method can allow clients to augment their local datasets (which may lack data from certain classes) with synthetically generated data using a learnt variational auto encoder and the shared means of some latent representation from other clients. In particular, the paper argues that by adding noise to the shared means, the method provides differential privacy. Empirical comparison with several baselines is provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

- The studied problem (i.e., how to address non-i.i.d. data in federated learning) is relevant and important.

- The comparison with existing works seems sufficient (in related work and experiments).

- The reproducibility of the paper is good (the experimental details are clearly documented and the code is also provided).


### Weaknesses

- Some assumptions and/or settings can be motivated better.
    - The specific definition of non-i.i.d. data can be explained more clearly and motivated better. The title, abstract, introduction and main body of the paper all mention non-i.i.d., but it is only specified in the experiments section for empirical verification. While it is informally mentioned that some clients may have class imbalanced data, it was not so clear the motivation for this specific non-i.i.d. setting. 
    - It is not so clear why the server can have partial information about the clients' data distributions. This assumption can be better motivated.
    > (in particular, indices of the most abundant and the least abundant classes)


- The focus of the paper may be spread too thin, in an attempt to address too many different challenges. In particular, the paper mentions domain generalization, client matching, differential privacy, all the while trying to address the effect of non-i.i.d. data distributions. It may be more to the point if the focus of the paper is sharpened to specifically address one challenge clearly and well. For instance, it is not so clear why non-i.i.d. setting must be addressed together with differential privacy. While I understand both are practical challenges faced in federated learning, is there a deeper theoretical connection that motivates jointly studying both? 


- Some design choices can be justified better, e.g., through theoretical guarantees.
    - The paper argues the mean sharing is differentially private, yet without providing theoretical results guaraneeting it. 
    - In the introduction:
    > our proposed framework relies on simple Variational Auto-Encoders (VAEs) well- suited to the classification tasks of interest.

        It is unclear why VAEs are better suited than GANs in this case.

    - The client matching method can be improved with a formal discussion. 
    > The matching is based on the distance between the clients’ data distributions.

        What is this distance, how does doing matching in this way help the clients to address the non-i.i.d. setting with theoretical backing related to that distance?

    - In section 3.1, the paper mentions that this method is potentially complementary to existing FL methods for non-i.i.d. data. So how should this paper be positioned against these existing methods? More specifically, what is/are the fundamental challenge(s) that the existing methods cannot resolve but this proposed method manages resolve?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
#### Clarity and Quality:

The writing is reasonable, though it can be a bit difficult to understand due to the many components of the designed method.

#### Novelty:

The proposed method combines some existing designs applied to FL such as VAEs, domain generalization and differential privacy. 

#### Reproducibility:

Reproducibility is good.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies a relevant problem. However, it may be better if the focus of the paper is sharpened to address one (or two) specific challenge(s) to provide deeper insights of the challenge(s) with corresponding theoretical results. Doing so could also help reader identify the position of this paper against existing works in terms of what are the fundamental challenges that are not addressed previously but effectively addressed by this paper. Hence, at current stage, another iteration of careful improvement is necessary.

content.title: Federated Learning in Non-IID Settings Aided by Differentially Private Synthetic Data
content.TL;DR: A novel federated learning framework utilizing data augmentation to improve global accuracy among data-heterogeneous clients
content.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a privacy-promoting framework that enables potentially large number of clients to collaboratively train machine learning models. In an FL system, a server coordinates the collaboration by collecting and aggregating clients' model updates while the clients' data remains local and private. A major challenge in federated learning arises when the local data is non-iid -- the setting in which performance of the learned global model may deteriorate significantly compared to the scenario where the data is identically distributed across the clients. In this paper we propose FedDPMS (Federated Differentially Private Means Sharing), an FL algorithm in which clients augment local datasets with data synthesized using differentially private information collected and communicated by a trusted server. In particular, the server matches the pairs of clients having complementary local datasets and facilitates differentially-private sharing of the means of latent data representations; the clients then deploy variational auto-encoders to enrich their datasets and thus ameliorate the effects of non-iid data distribution. Our experiments on deep image classification tasks demonstrate that FedDPMS outperforms competing state-of-the-art FL methods specifically developed to address the challenge of federated learning on non-iid data.
